title: Owls
objective: After this level you can explain how owls hunt in the dark.
summary: Barn owls can strike prey in total darkness by sound alone. Lopsided ears find a sound's height, a dish-shaped face funnels sound in, and muffled feathers keep the hunt quiet.

cards.headline: In 1958, an owl caught a paper wad in total darkness.
cards.body: Owls are the night shift of the birds of prey. Researchers Payne and Drury let a mouse tow a crumpled wad of paper through a pitch-dark room. The barn owl struck the paper. It couldn't see it, and paper doesn't smell like dinner. So how did it know where to strike?

cards.headline: Ears that aren't level
cards.body: It heard it. A barn owl's ears are lopsided, one slightly higher than the other. A sound from below comes in louder on one side, a sound from above on the other, so the owl can tell a sound's height as well as its direction. That pins prey down in three dimensions. Audubon says barn owls are better at finding prey by ear than any other animal tested.

cards.headline: A face shaped like a dish
cards.body: All owls have a facial disc, a ring of short feathers around the face. The barn owl's heart-shaped disc is especially prominent, and it works like a satellite dish, funneling sound toward the ears. That face you find so cute is mostly hearing equipment.

cards.fact: Owl wings are built to hush.
cards.context: Owl flight feathers have comb-like serrations along the front edge that break up the air, a velvety surface, and a soft fringe on the trailing edge. Together they damp the swoosh of flight. That may help twice: the prey can't hear the owl coming, and the owl can keep listening to the prey.

cards.headline: Owls: explained
learned: Barn owls can strike prey in total darkness by sound
Lopsided ears find a sound's height and direction
The facial disc funnels sound like a satellite dish
Serrated, velvety feathers muffle their flight

questions.prompt: In Payne and Drury's 1958 dark-room test, what did the barn owl strike?

options.label: The mouse, guided by its smell
options.rationale: Smell was ruled out; it struck what made the noise.

options.label: A dim light in the corner
Nothing; owls won't hunt in total darkness
options.rationale: It struck its target without any light.

questions.explanation: The owl struck the paper the mouse was towing, ruling out sight and smell: it hunted by sound.

questions.prompt: How does having one ear higher than the other help a barn owl hunt?

options.label: It lets the owl hear much higher pitches
options.rationale: The card is about where a sound is, not its pitch.

options.label: It keeps wind noise out while flying
options.rationale: Quiet flight comes from the feathers.

options.label: It tells the owl how high a sound is
It lets the owl turn its head farther
options.rationale: The lopsided ears are about locating sound.

questions.explanation: Uneven ears hear sounds from above and below differently, so the owl finds a sound's height as well as direction.

questions.prompt: Owls are Level 24's night-shift birds of prey. What helps an owl reach its prey unheard?

options.label: Extra-large talons that grip silently
options.rationale: Talons grab; the silence comes from the feathers.

options.label: A notched beak for a quick bite
Hollow bones that absorb sound
options.rationale: The muffling is in the feathers.

questions.explanation: Serrated front edges, a velvety surface and soft trailing fringes damp the sound of an owl's flight.
